Bayesian Sheaf Neural Networks

Patrick Gillespie Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: University of Tennessee Affiliation: Knoxville, TN 37996 Email: pgilles5@vols.utk.edu    Vasileios Maroulas Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: University of Tennessee Affiliation: Knoxville, TN 37996 Email: vasileios.maroulas@utk.edu    Ioannis Schizas Affiliation: DEVCOM ARL Affiliation: Army Research Lab Affiliation: Aberdeen, MD 21001 Email: ioannis.d.schizas.civ@army.mil
Abstract

Equipping graph neural networks with a convolution operation defined in terms of a cellular sheaf offers advantages for learning expressive representations of heterophilic graph data. The most flexible approach to constructing the sheaf is to learn it as part of the network as a function of the node features. However, this leaves the network potentially overly sensitive to the learned sheaf. As a counter-measure, we propose a variational approach to learning cellular sheaves within sheaf neural networks, yielding an architecture we refer to as a Bayesian sheaf neural network. As part of this work, we define a novel family of reparameterizable probability distributions on the rotation group S​O​(n)SO(n) using the Cayley transform. We evaluate the Bayesian sheaf neural network on several graph datasets, and show that our Bayesian sheaf models outperform deterministic sheaf models when training data is limited, and are less sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters.

Keywords: Cellular sheaf, Bayesian neural network, variational inference, Cayley transform

1 Introduction

Geometric and topological deep learning are rapidly developing research areas which, broadly speaking, aim to use geometric priors about the data of interest to develop neural network architectures using methods and tools from differential geometry, topology, and graph theory [12, 46]. Graph neural networks are a central example of geometric deep learning and have been applied to a wide range of tasks such as recommender systems [54], traffic modeling [42, 55], and predicting properties of chemicals [30]. Building on the basic idea of graph neural networks, architectures such as simplicial convolutional neural networks and hypergraph neural networks extend the graph convolution operation to a higher order convolution operation, which has advantages when the dataset contains salient relationships between groups of nodes rather than just pairs such as citation networks[20, 24], chemical data [8, 7], and neural data [44]. However, such convolution operators suffer from over-smoothing, and thus tend to perform best on homophilic graph data, where nodes connected together by edges or higher dimensional simplices have a high likelihood of belonging to the same class [50, 6].

Several approaches have been taken to address the limited capabilities of GCNs and higher-order variants for heterophilic graph data (i.e. not homophilic) [53, 48, 58, 57]. One approach replaces the graph (or simplicial) convolution operation with a convolution operation defined in terms of a cellular sheaf [32, 6]. A cellular sheaf, briefly, is a data structure defined on a simplicial complex which associates a vector space to each simplex, and a linear transformation known as a restriction map to each pair of incident simplices, that is, a pair of simplices where one simplex is a face of the other. The restriction maps provide additional flexibility in the message passing operation. They allow neighboring nodes to maintain distinct features throughout the layers of the sheaf neural network: an advantageous quality when working with heterophilic graph data.

While sheaf neural networks were developed to address the issue of over-smoothing in graph neural networks, they are still susceptible to many of the issues common to all neural networks, such as overfitting to limited training data and lack of robustness to noisy data, weight initializations, and hyperparameter selections. One approach to mitigating such issues is to apply tools and ideas from Bayesian statistics to deep learning [36, 47]. Bayesian approaches to machine learning have been used to quantify uncertainty of neural network predictions [38, 28], reduce overfitting [27, 29], add robustness to adversarial attacks [9], as well as simply improve the predictions of machine learning algorithms [22, 31, 43].

In this paper, we apply a Bayesian framework to learning cellular sheaves within a sheaf neural network. Specifically, we regard the sheaf Laplacian—an object which generalizes the graph Laplacian to cellular sheaves—as a latent random variable of the sheaf neural network.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We introduce Bayesian sheaf neural networks (BSNN) in which the sheaf Laplacian operator of the sheaf neural network is a latent random variable whose distribution is parameterized by a function of the input data. Motivated by the evidence lower bound for variational Bayesian inference, a pertinent loss function for our BSNN which contains a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term is derived to efficiently train the BSNN.

  2. 2.

    We define a novel family of reparameterizable probability distributions on the rotation group S​O​(n)SO(n) that we refer to as Cayley distributions. The Cayley distributions are reparameterizable and have tractable density functions, and thus can be used to perform variational inference on the sheaf Laplacian within the BSNN when the sheaf restriction maps belong to S​O​(n)SO(n). We derive closed-form expressions for the KL divergence of the Cayley distributions from the uniform distribution on S​O​(n)SO(n) when n=2,3n=2,3.

  3. 3.

    We evaluate BSNN models on several benchmark graph datasets, specifically, on node-classification tasks with limited training data.

1.1 Related Work

We first discuss existing work on sheaf neural networks. Sheaf neural networks (SNN) were first introduced in [32], where they were shown to outperform graph convolutional networks on a semi-supervised node classification task using a hand-selected cellular sheaf. A more in-depth investigation of sheaf neural networks, sheaf diffusion processes, and the advantage of SNNs for heterophilic graph data was performed in [6], where they also constructed a method of learning a suitable cellular sheaf from the data as part of the sheaf neural network. Variants of sheaf neural networks include SNNs with attention-based edge weights [3], and SNNs defined for hypergraphs rather than cellular complexes [19]. Besides hand-crafting a sheaf for a particular problem or learning a sheaf during training, Barbero et al. [2] construct a sheaf at preprocessing time by assuming the graph data lies on a low dimensional manifold and defining a cellular sheaf in a manner inspired by connections from differential geometry.

Although no existing work has applied a Bayesian framework to sheaf neural networks, we mention some of the ways in which Bayesian neural networks have been combined with geometric machine learning. A variational auto-encoder using graph convolutional layers was considered in [40] for an edge detection task. Davidson et al. [18] discuss variational auto-encoders where the latent variable takes values in a hypersphere. Hajiramezanali et al. [31] combine graph variational autoencoders with graph recurrent networks to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods on dynamic link prediction tasks. Beyond variational autoencoders, Fan et al. model attention weights in graph attention networks as random latent variables, as well as in other architectures which use attention [22]. Given that the inclusion or exclusion of edges in graph datasets can be due to spurious noise or modelling assumptions, Zhang et al. view graph datasets as realizations of parametric families of random graphs, and develop a Bayesian graph convolutional network accordingly [56].

Defining a distribution over cellular sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps requires a convenient family of distributions over S​O​(n)SO(n). The most well-known probability distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n) are the matrix Langevin (or von Mises-Fisher) distribution [45, 15] and the matrix Bingham distribution [14]. However such distributions are not easily reparameterizable, which makes incorporating them within neural networks trained via backpropagation difficult. Falorsi et al. [21] use the matrix exponential map to construct reparameterizable distributions on S​O​(d)SO(d), however, these distributions in general do not have tractable density functions. In this paper, we define a family of reparameterizable distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n) defined via the Cayley transform which we refer to as Cayley distributions. These are distinct from the Cayley distributions defined in [41], and we compare the two families of distributions in Section 4. We also mention [35], where a generalized version of the Cayley transform was used to simulate distributions on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds.

1.2 Overview

In Section 2, we review preliminary topics such as cellular sheaves and sheaf Laplacians. We review how the sheaf Laplacian can be used to define a sheaf neural network, and the connection to a sheaf diffusion process. We prove a result regarding the linear separation power of a sheaf diffusion process for sheaves consisting of special orthogonal maps. In Section 3, we describe our variational approach to learning cellular sheaves within a sheaf neural network. In Section 4, we define a reparameterizable family of distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n), which are used to define the variational distribution for cellular sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps. In Section 5, we evaluate our BSNN on several node classification tasks for heterophilic web-page datasets. We end with a final discussion, as well as potential directions for future work in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Cellular Sheaves

A kk−-simplex is the convex hull of k+1k+1 affinely independent points in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Familiar examples include points, lines, triangles, and tetrahedrons, which are 00, 11, 22, and 33−-simplices respectively. A face τ\tau of a simplex σ\sigma is the simplex spanned by any subset of the points defining σ\sigma. In this case we denote τ​⊴​σ\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma, and may say that τ\tau is incident with σ\sigma. A simplicial complex KK is a collection of simplices in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that for any simplex in KK, all of its faces are also in KK, and whenever two simplices σ,τ\sigma,\tau in KK have a non-empty intersection σ∩τ\sigma\cap\tau, their intersection is a face of both σ\sigma and τ\tau.

A cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} on a simplicial complex KK is a structure which assigns a vector space ℱ⁡(σ)\mathcal{F}(\sigma) to each simplex σ∈K\sigma\in K, and assigns to each incident pair τ​⊴​σ\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma a linear transformation ℱτ​⊴​σ:ℱ⁡(τ)→ℱ⁡(σ)\mathcal{F}_{\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma}:\mathcal{F}(\tau)\to\mathcal{F}(\sigma) such that ℱσ​⊴​σ:ℱ⁡(σ)→ℱ⁡(σ)\mathcal{F}_{\sigma\trianglelefteq\sigma}:\mathcal{F}(\sigma)\to\mathcal{F}(\sigma) is the identity map for every σ\sigma, and with the compatibility condition that ℱτ​⊴​ρ=ℱσ​⊴​ρ∘ℱτ​⊴​σ\mathcal{F}_{\tau\trianglelefteq\rho}=\mathcal{F}_{\sigma\trianglelefteq\rho}\circ\mathcal{F}_{\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma} whenever τ​⊴​σ​⊴​ρ\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma\trianglelefteq\rho. In keeping with the terminology from sheaf theory [11], the vector space ℱ⁡(σ)\mathcal{F}(\sigma) is referred to as the stalk of ℱ\mathcal{F} over σ\sigma, and the transformations ℱτ​⊴​σ\mathcal{F}_{\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma} are referred to as restriction maps. Cellular sheaves can be defined on cell complexes, a slight generalization of simplicial complexes, hence their name. For simplicity of presentation, we restrict our attention to simplicial complexes.

The motivation for considering cellular sheaves in the context of geometric deep learning is that given a cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}, there is a corresponding sheaf Laplacian LℱL_{\mathcal{F}}. Just as how the message passing operation in many graph convolutional neural networks is defined in terms of the graph Laplacian L=D−AL=D-A [40], the sheaf Laplacian LℱL_{\mathcal{F}} can be used to define a message passing operation.

To begin defining the sheaf Laplacian for a cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} over a finite simplicial complex KK, assume a total order is placed on the vertices of KK, so that each simplex σ∈K\sigma\in K may be written σ=[v0,v1,…,vn]\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{n}] with v0<v1<⋯<vnv_{0}<v_{1}<\cdots<v_{n}. Given a kk−-simplex σ=[v0,v1,…,vk]\sigma=[v_{0},v_{1},\dots,v_{k}], we denote its (k−1)(k-1)−-dimensional faces by ∂i(σ):=[v0,…,v^i,…,vk]\partial_{i}(\sigma):=[v_{0},\dots,\hat{v}_{i},\dots,v_{k}] for i∈{0,…,k}i\in\{0,\dots,k\}, where v^i\hat{v}_{i} denotes the omission of vertex viv_{i}.

An nn−-cochain of (K,ℱ)(K,\mathcal{F}) is an element x∈Cn​(K,ℱ)x\in C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F}), where Cn​(K,ℱ):=⨁σ∈Knℱ⁡(σ)C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F}):=\bigoplus_{\sigma\in K_{n}}\mathcal{F}(\sigma) denotes the direct sum of the vector spaces ℱ⁡(σ)\mathcal{F}(\sigma) over all nn−-dimensional simplices σ∈Kn\sigma\in K_{n}. Given a cochain x∈Cn​(K,ℱ)x\in C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F}) and an nn−-simplex σ\sigma, let xσx_{\sigma} denote the value of xx at ℱ⁡(σ)\mathcal{F}(\sigma), i.e. xσ=πσ​(x)x_{\sigma}=\pi_{\sigma}(x) for the projection πσ:Cn​(K,ℱ)→ℱ⁡(σ)\pi_{\sigma}:C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F})\to\mathcal{F}(\sigma). The nn−-th coboundary map δn:Cn​(K,ℱ)→Cn+1​(K,ℱ)\delta_{n}:C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F})\to C^{n+1}(K;\mathcal{F}) is the linear transformation given by defining the value of δn​(x)\delta_{n}(x) at an (n+1)(n+1)−-simplex σ\sigma to be

δn​(x)σ=∑i=0n+1(−1)i​ℱ∂iσ​⊴​σ​((x)∂iσ).\delta_{n}(x)_{\sigma}=\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^{i}\mathcal{F}_{\partial_{i}\sigma\trianglelefteq\sigma}((x)_{\partial_{i}\sigma}). (1)

The nn−-th sheaf Laplacian of (K,ℱ)(K,\mathcal{F}) is the linear transformation Lℱn:Cn​(K,ℱ)→Cn​(K,ℱ)L_{\mathcal{F}}^{n}:C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F})\to C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F}) defined by

Lℱn=δn−1​δn−1∗+δn∗​δn,L^{n}_{\mathcal{F}}=\delta_{n-1}\delta_{n-1}^{*}+\delta_{n}^{*}\delta_{n}, (2)

where δn∗:Cn+1​(K,ℱ)→Cn​(K,ℱ)\delta_{n}^{*}:C^{n+1}(K;\mathcal{F})\to C^{n}(K;\mathcal{F}) denotes the adjoint of δn\delta_{n}. In the case that ℱ⁡(σ)=ℝ\mathcal{F}(\sigma)=\mathbb{R} for all σ∈K\sigma\in K and ℱτ​⊴​σ\mathcal{F}_{\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma} is the identity map on ℝ\mathbb{R} for all pairs τ​⊴​σ\tau\trianglelefteq\sigma, the nn−-th sheaf Laplacian LℱnL_{\mathcal{F}}^{n} is simply the combinatorial Laplacian of the simplicial complex KK [25]. For further information on cellular sheaves and sheaf Laplacians, we refer the interested reader to [33].

2.1.1 Cellular Sheaves over Graphs

Although the sheaf Laplacians LℱnL_{\mathcal{F}}^{n} for multiple dimensions nn could be used as message passing operations within a sheaf neural network, due to the prevalence of graph-based data, one is primarily concerned with cellular sheaves over graphs, which are 11−-dimensional simplicial complexes, and the 00th sheaf Laplacian Lℱ0L_{\mathcal{F}}^{0}, denoted by LℱL_{\mathcal{F}}.

Given a sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} over a graph GG with nn nodes, and assuming the stalk ℱ⁡(u)\mathcal{F}(u) over each node u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) has the same dimension dd, the sheaf Laplacian, Lℱ,L_{\mathcal{F}}, may be represented as a block matrix of size n​d×n​dnd\times nd. The off-diagonal blocks Li​j∈ℝd×dL_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are Li​j=−ℱuj​⊴​e𝖳​ℱui​⊴​e,L_{ij}=-\mathcal{F}_{u_{j}\trianglelefteq e}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{F}_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}, whenever there exists an edge between the nodes uiu_{i} and uju_{j}, and Li​j=0L_{ij}=0 otherwise. The diagonal blocks are Li​i=∑ui​⊴​eℱui​⊴​e𝖳​ℱui​⊴​e,L_{ii}=\sum_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}\mathcal{F}_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{F}_{u_{i}\trianglelefteq e}, where the sum is over all edges ee such that ui​⊴​eu_{i}\trianglelefteq e. If we let DD denote the n​d×n​dnd\times nd block diagonal matrix whose diagonal blocks are Li​iL_{ii}, and all other blocks are zero matrices, then the normalized 00th sheaf Laplacian Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}} defined in [32] is Δℱ:=D−1/2LℱD−1/2.\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}:=D^{-1/2}L_{\mathcal{F}}D^{-1/2}. Note DD is symmetric positive semi-definite, hence there exists a matrix D1/2D^{1/2} such that D1/2​D1/2=DD^{1/2}D^{1/2}=D. Moreover, we only consider sheaves such that the restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} are invertible, in which case DD is invertible, and so D−1/2D^{-1/2} is well-defined.

2.2 Sheaf Diffusion

Let GG be a graph with nn nodes and with dd−-dimensional node features, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a cellular sheaf over GG with dd−-dimensional stalks. We represent the node features as an n​dnd−-dimensional vector X∈ℝn​dX\in\mathbb{R}^{nd} so that the normalized sheaf Laplacian Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}, as a n​d×n​dnd\times nd block matrix, updates XX by matrix-vector multiplication Δℱ​X\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}X. Motivated by how the graph convolutional layers of [40] can be viewed as a discretization of a heat diffusion process dd​t​X​(t)=−Δ​X​(t)\tfrac{d}{dt}X(t)=-\Delta X(t) defined in terms of the normalized graph Laplacian Δ\Delta, the authors of [6] consider a similar diffusion process which now uses the sheaf Laplacian:

X⁡(0)=X,dd​t​X​(t)=−Δℱ​X​(t).X(0)=X,\quad\tfrac{d}{dt}X(t)=-\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}X(t). (3)

Applying the Euler method with unit time-steps to approximate solutions to Eq. (3) yields

X⁡(t+1)=X⁡(t)−Δℱ​X​(t).X(t+1)=X(t)-\Delta_{\mathcal{F}}X(t). (4)

The authors of [6] use Eq. (4) to define sheaf diffusion layers as follows. Allowing for f∈ℕf\in\mathbb{N} distinct feature channels, let X∈ℝn​d×fX\in\mathbb{R}^{nd\times f} be a feature matrix. Given a sheaf Laplacian operator Δℱ⁡(t)\Delta_{\mathcal{F}(t)} for layer tt, a sheaf diffusion layer is defined by setting

Xt+1=Xt−σ⁡(Δℱ⁡(t)​(In⊗Wt,1)​Xt​Wt,2).X_{t+1}=X_{t}-\sigma\big(\Delta_{\mathcal{F}(t)}(I_{n}\otimes W_{t,1})X_{t}W_{t,2}\big). (5)

Here Wt,1∈ℝd×dW_{t,1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and Wt,2∈ℝf×fW_{t,2}\in\mathbb{R}^{f\times f} are weight matrices for layer tt, σ\sigma is a non-linear activation function, ⊗\otimes denotes a Kronecker product.

As a measure of the expressive power of sheaf layers based on Eq. (4), Bodnar et al. [6] study the ability of the sheaf diffusion process in Eq. (3) to linearly separate the features of nodes belonging to different classes.

Definition 2.1.

A class of sheaves ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} with dd−-dimensional stalks is said to have linear separation power over a class of labeled graphs 𝒢\mathcal{G} if for every G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G}, there exists a sheaf ℱ∈ℋd\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{H}^{d} such that the sheaf diffusion process determined by ℱ\mathcal{F} on GG linearly separates the features X⁡(t)X(t) of the classes of GG in the time limit t→∞t\to\infty, for almost all initial conditions X⁡(0)X(0).

As part of a sheaf learning mechanism within a sheaf neural network, a fixed class of sheaves ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} is parameterized, and the input data is mapped to a suitable sheaf ℱ∈ℋd\mathcal{F}\in\mathcal{H}^{d} through this parameterization. For a node classification task with CC classes, the collection of sheaves ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} used would ideally have linear separation power over the collection of connected graphs with CC classes. While one could always take ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} to be as general as possible, it can be preferable to use a more restricted collection of sheaves, as this can reduce the number of model parameters involved in learning a cellular sheaf. For example, learning cellular sheaves whose restriction maps are diagonal or special orthogonal matrices involves fewer parameters than when the restriction maps are general linear maps. Recall that a special orthogonal matrix, i.e. element of S​O​(n)SO(n), is a matrix QQ such that QT=Q−1Q^{T}=Q^{-1} and det(Q)=1\det(Q)=1.

It was shown that the class of sheaves ℋdiagd\mathcal{H}^{d}_{\diag} with invertible diagonal restriction maps has linear separation power over the collection 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} of connected graphs with CC classes whenever C≤dC\leq d [6]. However, for ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d}, the class of sheaves with d×dd\times d special orthogonal restriction maps, [6, Proposition 13] only guarantees the existence of a dd such that ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} when C≤8C\leq 8.

Remark 2.2.

In [6], sheaves with orthogonal restriction maps, rather than special orthogonal, are considered. However, since the sheaf learning mechanism in their SNN is a continuous parametrization of the orthogonal group O⁡(n)O(n) by the connected space ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, it must have its image contained in a connected component of O⁡(n)O(n). Given that this implies that the restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} will either all have determinant 11 or all have determinant −1-1, the maps ℱu​⊴​e𝖳​ℱv​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathcal{F}_{v\trianglelefteq e} used to define the sheaf Laplacian must always have determinant equal to 11. Thus it is effectively equivalent to learning restriction maps belonging to S​O​(n)SO(n).

The class of sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps is of particular interest for sheaf neural networks—including our Bayesian sheaf neural networks—due to both theoretical and practical properties. From the theoretical point of view, certain results concerning the kernel of Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}} can be proven for sheaves using rotations as restriction maps [6, Section 3.1]. Regarding the more practical aspects, rotations offer a nice middle-ground between diagonal and general linear map in terms of balancing the number of parameters with the expressivity of the resulting sheaf. Moreover, when using rotations, the blocks along the diagonal of the sheaf Laplacian LℱL_{\mathcal{F}} are scalar multiples of the identity matrix. This makes computing the normalized sheaf Laplacian Δℱ\Delta_{\mathcal{F}} easier. Because of this, we take a moment to improve existing results on the linear separation power of the class of sheaves ℋs​od\mathcal{H}^{d}_{so} with d×dd\times d special orthogonal restriction maps. In particular, we prove that for any C∈ℕC\in\mathbb{N}, we may find dd large enough such that ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C}. In the following proposition, ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the floor function.

Proposition 2.3.

For any d≥1d\geq 1, if 𝒢\mathcal{G} denotes the class of connected graphs with C≤7​⌊d4⌋C\leq 7\lfloor\tfrac{d}{4}\rfloor classes, then ℋs​od\mathcal{H}_{so}^{d} has linear separation power over 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

For a proof see Appendix A.

Remark 2.4.

An extra consequence of Proposition 2.3 is that it also provides a new upper bound on the stalk dimension dd necessary for ℋg​e​nd\mathcal{H}^{d}_{gen}, the collection of sheaves with d×dd\times d general linear restriction maps, to have linear separation power over the collection of connected graph 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C} with CC classes. This is due to the simple fact that ℋs​od⊆ℋg​e​nd\mathcal{H}^{d}_{so}\subseteq\mathcal{H}^{d}_{gen}.

3 Bayesian Sheaf Neural Networks

We briefly establish some notation. Let PP be a distribution on a measurable space 𝒳\mathcal{X} with density pp with respect to some reference measure μ\mu. If XX is a random variable with distribution PP, we write X∼PX\sim P. For a function f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, we denote by 𝔼P​[f​(X)]\mathbb{E}_{P}[f(X)] the expectation of f⁡(X)f(X) with respect to the distribution PP, that is, 𝔼P​[f⁡(X)]=∫𝒳p⁡(x)​f​(x)​μ​(𝑑x)\mathbb{E}_{P}[f(X)]=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(x)f(x)\,\mu(dx). If QQ is another distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and QQ has density qq with respect to μ\mu, the Kullback-Leibler divergence of PP from QQ is

KL(P∥Q)=∫𝒳p(x)log(p⁡(x)q⁡(x))μ(dx).\textnormal{KL}(P\;\|\;Q)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p(x)\log\Bigg(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\Bigg)\,\mu(dx).

To simplify notation, we will denote a distribution by its density function. For instance, an expression of the form X∼p⁡(X|Y)X\sim p(X|Y) denotes that the random variable XX is distributed according to the conditional distribution of XX given YY.

3.1 Problem Statement

Consider a semi-supervised node classification problem, in which we have a graph dataset G=(V,E)G=(V,E) together with a node feature matrix XX, a collection of observed node labels, yy, and a collection of unobserved node labels y∗y^{*}, all of which are random samples. Motivated by the expressive power of the sheaf diffusion process, we model the conditional probability pθ​(y|X)p_{\theta}(y|X) using a sheaf neural network whose layers are given by Eq. 5, with network parameters θ\theta and a cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Rather than take the learned cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} (or sheaves) to be a deterministic function of XX as in [6], we instead regard ℱ\mathcal{F} as a latent random variable of our model. See Figure 1 for a depiction of the probability graphical model. Note that the posterior distribution pθ​(ℱ|X,y)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) will be intractable due to the fact that the labels yy are modeled as the output of a neural network. Hence, to do approximate posterior inference of ℱ\mathcal{F} given the feature matrix, XX, the observed node labels yy, and model parameters θ\theta, we assume the intractable posterior distribution pθ​(ℱ|X,y)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) belongs to a predetermined family of variational distributions qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) parameterized by weights ϕ\phi.

We begin by noting that the log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(X,y)\log p_{\theta}(X,y) can be written

logpθ(X,y)=KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ|X,y))+ℒ(θ,ϕ;X,y),\log p_{\theta}(X,y)=\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y))+\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y), (6)

where

ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ,X,y):=𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)​[−log⁡qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)+log⁡pθ​(ℱ,X,y)].\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y):=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}\big[-\log q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)+\log p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F},X,y)\big]. (7)

The quantity ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ,X,y)\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y) is known as the evidence lower bound or ELBO, due to the fact that the KL divergence from one distribution to another is always non-negative, hence log⁡pθ​(X,y)≥ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ,X,y)\log p_{\theta}(X,y)\geq\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi,X,y). Note from Eq. (6) that maximizing the ELBO with respect to the parameters θ\theta and ϕ\phi has the effect of maximizing the log-likelihood of the data, as well as minimizing the KL divergence of the variational distribution qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) from the true posterior distribution pθ​(ℱ|X,y)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}|X,y). For this reason, the ELBO is commonly used as quantity to be optimized within variational Bayesian inference. See [5] for an overview of variational inference. In order to maximize ℒ⁡(θ,ϕ,X,y)\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y) with respect to the parameters θ,ϕ\theta,\phi, we use the following equivalent expression:

ℒ(θ,ϕ;X,y)=𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)[logpθ(X,y|ℱ)]−KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ)).\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}\big[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})\big]-\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})). (8)

In many cases, a closed-form expression can be derived for the KL-divergence term in the right hand side of Eq. (8), leaving only the gradient of the expectation term with respect to θ\theta and ϕ\phi to be estimated. See Appendix C for calculations of the KL divergence in certain cases. Similar to [39], we estimate ∇ϕ𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)​[log⁡pθ​(X,y|ℱ)]\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})] by making use of the so-called reparameterization trick. In our case, for a random cellular sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} distributed as ℱ∼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)\mathcal{F}\sim q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y), the reparameterization trick expresses ℱ\mathcal{F} as a deterministic function ℱ=gϕ​(ϵ,X)\mathcal{F}=g_{\phi}(\epsilon,X) of random noise ϵ∼p⁡(ϵ)\epsilon\sim p(\epsilon). This allows us to rewrite the expectation with respect to qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) as an expectation with respect to p⁡(ϵ)p(\epsilon) which in turn allows the gradient to be moved within the expectation. That is,

∇ϕ𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)​[log⁡pθ​(X,y|ℱ)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F})] =∇ϕ𝔼p⁡(ϵ)​[log⁡pθ​(X,y|gϕ​(ϵ,X))]\displaystyle=\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{p(\epsilon)}[\log p_{\theta}(X,y|g_{\phi}(\epsilon,X))]
=𝔼p⁡(ϵ)​[∇ϕ​log​pθ​(X,y|gϕ​(ϵ,X))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(\epsilon)}[\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\theta}(X,y|g_{\phi}(\epsilon,X))]
≈1K​∑k=1K∇ϕ​log​pθ​(X,y|gϕ​(ϵ(k),X)),\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\nabla_{\phi}\log p_{\theta}(X,y|g_{\phi}(\epsilon^{(k)},X)),

where ϵ(k)\epsilon^{(k)} are independent and identically distributed samples of p⁡(ϵ)p(\epsilon) for k∈{1,2,…,K}k\in\{1,2,\dots,K\}.

Hence, when the KL divergence term of Eq. (8) can be computed analytically, if ℱ(k)=gϕ​(ϵ(k),X)\mathcal{F}^{(k)}=g_{\phi}(\epsilon^{(k)},X) for ϵ(k)∼p⁡(ϵ)\epsilon^{(k)}\sim p(\epsilon), our estimator is

ℒ~λ(θ,ϕ;X,y)=1K∑k=1Klogpθ(X,y|ℱ(k))−λKL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ)).\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F}^{(k)})-\lambda\,\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})). (9)

Here, the weight λ\lambda of the KL divergence term is included to combat issues with the KL divergence term vanishing during training, which we cyclically anneal during training in a manner similar to [26]. When the KL divergence term of Eq. (8) cannot be computed analytically, we may estimate it in a similar manner by noting that KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ))=𝔼qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)[log(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)/pθ(ℱ))]\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}))=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)}[\log(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)/p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}))]. In this case, the estimator, also denoted by ℒ~λ\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}, is given by

ℒ~λ​(θ,ϕ,X,y)=1K​∑k=1K(log⁡pθ​(X,y|ℱ(k))−λ​log⁡qϕ​(ℱ(k)|X,y)pθ​(ℱ(k))),\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{\lambda}(\theta,\phi;X,y)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big(\log p_{\theta}(X,y|\mathcal{F}^{(k)})-\lambda\log\frac{q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}^{(k)}|X,y)}{p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}^{(k)})}\Big), (10)

where again, ℱ(k)=gϕ​(ϵ(k),X)\mathcal{F}^{(k)}=g_{\phi}(\epsilon^{(k)},X) for ϵ(k)∼p⁡(ϵ)\epsilon^{(k)}\sim p(\epsilon).

3.2 Variational Sheaf Learner

We consider a variational sheaf learner in three different cases: where the learned sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} has restriction maps which are assumed to be (1) general linear, (2) special orthogonal, or (3) invertible diagonal. In all cases, we make the simplifying assumption that the variational distribution qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) from the previous section factors as the product ∏u​⊴​eqϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) over all incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e. While this assumption somewhat restricts the family of variational distributions, it makes computing the KL divergence term in the ELBO tractable. For further details, see Appendix C. We take each factor qϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) to be a distribution Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) which depends on the type of restriction map used within the sheaf, where the distributional parameters μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are a function of the node features XX and ϕ\phi as follows. For each incident node-edge pair u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e, if u′​⊴​eu^{\prime}\trianglelefteq e denotes the other node incident with ee, a multi-layer perceptron with learned weights ϕ\phi, denoted MLPϕ\MLP_{\phi}, maps the concatenated vector [xu||xu′][x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}] to distributional parameters μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}:

[μu​⊴​e||σu​⊴​e]=MLPϕ([xu||xu′]).[\,\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\,||\,\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\,]=\MLP_{\phi}([x_{u}||x_{u^{\prime}}]). (11)

Recall that a multi-layer perceptron is the composition of several feed-forward layers, each of which is a function of the form x↦σ⁡(W​x+b)x\mapsto\sigma(Wx+b), where σ\sigma is a nonlinear activation function, in our case the exponential linear unit (ELU) [16], WW is a weight matrix, and bb is a vector of biases.

Case 1: General Linear. In the case where the sheaf restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e:ℱ⁡(u)→ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(u)\to\mathcal{F}(e) are general linear maps, μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are d2d^{2}−-dimensional vectors. We take Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) to be normal with diagonal covariance so that for z∼𝒩d2​(μu​⊴​e,diag⁡(σu​⊴​e))z\sim\mathcal{N}_{d^{2}}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})) we set ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e} to be the vector zz rearranged into a d×dd\times d matrix. The reparameterization trick in this case writes z=μu​⊴​e+diag⁡(σu​⊴​e)​ϵz=\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}+\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})\epsilon for ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,Id2)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_{d^{2}}) so that ℱu​⊴​e\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}, being the matrix obtained by reshaping the vector zz, is a deterministic function of μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}, σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}, and ϵ\epsilon. We use a standard normal prior, where pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) and pθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)=𝒩d2​(𝟎,Id2)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{N}_{d^{2}}(\mathbf{0},I_{d^{2}}).

Case 2: Special Orthogonal. The case where sheaf restriction maps are assumed to be special orthogonal presents challenges. Typical probability distribution on S​O​(d)SO(d), such as the matrix Langevin distribution, are not easily reparameterizable. This makes incorporating such distributions into neural networks, that are trained via back-propagation, difficult. On the other hand, while reparameterizable distributions on S​O​(d)SO(d) have been constructed in [21] using the exponential map, the density functions of such distributions can be difficult to compute exactly, which obstructs one from computing, or even efficiently estimating, the KL divergence term in Eq. (8). In Section 4 we define what we refer to as Cayley distributions, a family of reparameterizable distributions 𝒞d​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) on S​O​(d)SO(d) with closed form expressions for their probability density functions. We use 𝒞d​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{d}(M,\kappa) as the variational distributions for sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps. Hence when ℱu​⊴​e∈S​O​(d)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d), the distributional parameters are a mean rotation μu​⊴​e∈S​O​(d)\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in SO(d) and scalar concentration parameter σu​⊴​e∈[0,1)\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\in[0,1), and we have Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)=𝒞d​(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{C}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}). The reparameterization of the Cayley distributions is described in Remark 4.3. We use a prior distribution pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) where each pθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) is a uniform distribution on S​O​(d)SO(d).

Case 3: Invertible Diagonal. In the case where the sheaf restriction maps ℱu​⊴​e:ℱ⁡(u)→ℱ⁡(e)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}:\mathcal{F}(u)\to\mathcal{F}(e) are assumed to be invertible diagonal matrices with respect to the standard basis, μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} are dd−-dimensional vectors and we take qϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)=Q⁡(μu​⊴​e,σu​⊴​e)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)=Q(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}) to be a normal distribution with diagonal covariance, so that ℱu​⊴​e=diag⁡(z)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\diag(z) for z∼𝒩d​(μu​⊴​e,diag⁡(σu​⊴​e))z\sim\mathcal{N}_{d}(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e},\diag(\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e})). The reparameterization ℱ=gϕ​(X,ϵ)\mathcal{F}=g_{\phi}(X,\epsilon) in this case is given by setting ℱu​⊴​e=diag⁡(μu​⊴​e+σu​⊴​e​ϵ)\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}=\diag(\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e}+\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e}\epsilon) for ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,Id)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},I_{d}). Lastly, we use a standard normal prior, where pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}) and pθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)=𝒩d​(𝟎,Id)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})=\mathcal{N}_{d}(\mathbf{0},I_{d}).

3.3 Bayesian Sheaf Neural Network Overview

We give an overview of the Bayesian sheaf neural network architecture, which is also summarized in 2. The variational sheaf learning mechanism maps the input node features to the sheaf distributional parameters as described in Section 3.2, though we briefly describe here as well. A linear layer first resizes the input node features to dimension kk. Specifically, we use k=d​fk=df where dd and ff are the stalk dimensions and number of feature channels respectively. Then, for each incident node-edge pair u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e, the features of the pair of nodes corresponding to the edge ee are concatenated. Hence a node feature matrix of size n×kn\times k is transformed by this concatenation operation into a matrix of size 2​e×2​k2e\times 2k, where nn denotes the number of nodes, and ee denotes the number of edges in the graph. Lastly, an MLP maps these features indexed by the incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e to distributional parameters μu​⊴​e\mu_{u\trianglelefteq e} and σu​⊴​e\sigma_{u\trianglelefteq e} as described by Eq. (11), which define the distribution over the cellular sheaves. From this distribution, a collection of independent and identically distributed sheaves ℱ1,ℱ2,…,ℱL\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L} are sampled: one for each layer of the network.

Separately, a multi-layer perceptron maps the input node features X∈ℝn×mX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} to features of dimension X′∈ℝn×d​fX^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times df} where dd is the stalk dimension and ff is the number of hidden channels. The features X′X^{\prime} are reshaped to size n​d×fnd\times f. Sheaf layers described by Eq. (5) update the transformed features X′X^{\prime} using the sampled sheaves ℱ1,ℱ2,…,ℱL\mathcal{F}_{1},\mathcal{F}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{L}. Finally, a linear layer maps the output of the final sheaf layer to a vector of class probabilities.

During training, a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of Eq. (9) or Eq. (10) is computed, and the loss is back-propagated to update the network weights. During testing, ensembling is performed to obtain point estimates for the unobserved node labels y∗y^{*}.

4 Reparameterizable Distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n)

In order to perform variational inference for our BSNN when cellular sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps are used, we require a family of distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n) that are both reparameterizable and have tractable density functions. We define a novel family of such distributions via the Cayley transform [13].

4.1 Cayley Distributions on S​O​(n)SO(n)

We denote the set of all n×nn\times n skew-symmetric matrices by 𝔰​𝔬​(n)\mathfrak{so}(n). The Cayley transform is a function C:𝔰​𝔬​(n)→S​O​(n)C:\mathfrak{so}(n)\to SO(n) defined by

C⁡(A)=(I−A)−1​(I+A)=2​(I−A)−1−I.C(A)=(I-A)^{-1}(I+A)=2(I-A)^{-1}-I. (12)

If AA is an n×nn\times n skew-symmetric matrix, then x𝖳​A​x=0x^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=0 for all x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} due to the fact that x𝖳​A​x=(x𝖳​A​x)𝖳=−x𝖳​A​xx^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=(x^{\mathsf{T}}Ax)^{\mathsf{T}}=-x^{\mathsf{T}}Ax. Hence if (I−A)​x=0(I-A)x=0, then x𝖳​(I−A)​x=x𝖳​x=0x^{\mathsf{T}}(I-A)x=x^{\mathsf{T}}x=0 implying that x=0x=0. Thus I−AI-A is invertible, showing that the Cayley transform is well-defined. If P∈S​O​(n)P\in SO(n) does not have −1-1 as an eigenvalue, C−1​(P)C^{-1}(P) exists and is given by

C−1​(P)=(P−I)​(I+P)−1=I−2​(I+P)−1.C^{-1}(P)=(P-I)(I+P)^{-1}=I-2(I+P)^{-1}. (13)

Hence CC is injective, and all but a measure zero subset of S​O​(n)SO(n) is contained in the image of CC.

Remark 4.1.

The Cayley transform is sometimes alternatively defined as C⁡(A)=(I+A)−1​(I−A)=(I−A)​(I+A)−1C(A)=(I+A)^{-1}(I-A)=(I-A)(I+A)^{-1}. Since the two definitions differ only by the precomposition of CC with the reflection A↦−AA\mapsto-A, either choice of definition could be used without meaningful change.

For a vector ϕ∈ℝn⁡(n−1)/2\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n(n-1)/2}, let XϕX_{\phi} denote the skew symmetric matrix containing the entries of ϕ\phi as its lower triangular entries. Explicitly, if ϕ=(ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕn⁡(n−1)/2)\phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\dots,\phi_{n(n-1)/2}) and if xi​jx_{ij} denotes the i,ji,j−-th entry of XϕX_{\phi}, then for i>ji>j, set xi​j=−xj​i=ϕi​j−j⁡(j+1)/2x_{ij}=-x_{ji}=\phi_{ij-j(j+1)/2} and set xi​i=0x_{ii}=0. We may vectorize the Cayley transform and regard it as a map C~:ℝn⁡(n−1)/2→ℝn2\widetilde{C}:\mathbb{R}^{n(n-1)/2}\to\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}} by setting C~​(ϕ)=vec⁡C⁡(Xϕ)\widetilde{C}(\phi)=\vect C(X_{\phi}). The Jacobian (determinant) of C~\widetilde{C} is J​C~​(ϕ)=det(D​C~​(ϕ)𝖳​D​C~​(ϕ))1/2J\widetilde{C}(\phi)=\det(D\widetilde{C}(\phi)^{\mathsf{T}}D\widetilde{C}(\phi))^{1/2}, where D​C~​(ϕ)D\widetilde{C}(\phi) denotes the total derivative of C~\widetilde{C} at the point ϕ\phi. The Jacobian J​C~​(ϕ)J\widetilde{C}(\phi) can be expressed [41] in terms of XϕX_{\phi} by

J​C~​(ϕ)=23​n​(n−1)/4det(I+Xϕ)n−1.J\widetilde{C}(\phi)=\frac{2^{3n(n-1)/4}}{\det(I+X_{\phi})^{n-1}}. (14)
Definition 4.2.

Let C:𝔰​𝔬​(n)→S​O​(n)C:\mathfrak{so}(n)\to SO(n) denote the Cayley transform and let XX be a uniformly distributed random variable on S​O​(n)SO(n). Given parameters M∈S​O​(n)M\in SO(n) and 0≤κ<10\leq\kappa<1, we define the Cayley distribution 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) on S​O​(n)SO(n) to be the distribution of Y=C⁡(1−κ1+κ​C−1​(X))​MY=C(\frac{1-\kappa}{1+\kappa}C^{-1}(X))M.

Remark 4.3.

Note that by the definition of the Cayley distribution, a random variable Y∼𝒞n​(M,κ)Y\sim\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) can be expressed as a deterministic function of MM, κ\kappa, and X∼US​O​(n)X\sim U_{SO(n)}. Hence these distributions are reparameterizable. For details on sampling from the uniform distribution on S​O​(n)SO(n), see for example [1].

In order to compute or efficiently estimate the KL divergence term in Eq. (9), an expression for the density of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) is necessary. Using Eq. (14) for the Jacobian of the Cayley transform, we compute the density of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) in the following theorem.

Theorem 4.4.

The Cayley distribution 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) has density

fn​(P,M,κ)=(1−κ2)n⁡(n−1)2​det(P​M𝖳−κ​I)1−n,f_{n}(P;M,\kappa)=(1-\kappa^{2})^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\det\Big(PM^{\mathsf{T}}-\kappa I\Big)^{1-n}, (15)

with respect to the normalized Haar measure on S​O​(n)SO(n).

For a proof see Appendix B.

Remark 4.5.

The family of Cayley distributions defined in [41] have density proportional to det(P​M𝖳+I)κ\det(PM^{\mathsf{T}}+I)^{\kappa} of Eq. (15). Note that the concentration parameter κ\kappa appears in the exponent of the determinant expression, whereas in our proposed family of Cayley distributions, κ\kappa instead scales the identity matrix term within the determinant.

4.2 Special Cases of the Cayley Distribution

We now examine the distributions 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) for small values of nn.

Case 𝐧=𝟐\mathbf{n=2}. If P,M∈S​O​(2)P,M\in SO(2) are rotations by θ,μ\theta,\mu radians respectively, then 𝒞2​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{2}(M,\kappa) has density

f2​(P,M,κ)=12​π⋅1−κ21+κ2−2​κ​cos⁡(θ−μ).f_{2}(P;M,\kappa)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{1-\kappa^{2}}{1+\kappa^{2}-2\kappa\cos(\theta-\mu)}.

This is the density of a wrapped Cauchy distribution on S​O​(2)≅S1SO(2)\cong S^{1}, see[37]. Hence for the case n=2n=2, the Cayley distributions coincide with known distributions.

Case 𝐧=𝟑\mathbf{n=3}. Note that S​O​(3)SO(3) is homeomorphic to 33−-dimensional real projective space R​P3RP^{3}, which is the quotient of S3S^{3} under the identification of antipodal points. We show that 𝒞3​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa) is related to an angular central Gaussian distribution [52] on S3S^{3}. Specifically, we show that 𝒞3​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa) is the pushforward of an angular central Gaussian distribution on S3S^{3} under the quotient map Φ:S3→S​O​(3)\Phi:S^{3}\to SO(3). If x∈ℝn+1x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1} is a unit vector, Λ∈ℝ(n+1)×(n+1)\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)} is a symmetric positive definite matrix, and αn\alpha_{n} denotes the volume of the nn−-dimensional sphere SnS^{n}, the angular central Gaussian distribution A​C​Gn​(Λ)ACG_{n}(\Lambda) on SnS^{n} has density

f⁡(x,Λ)=αn−1​det(Λ)−12​(x𝖳​Λ−1​x)−2f(x;\Lambda)=\alpha_{n}^{-1}\det(\Lambda)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(x^{\mathsf{T}}\Lambda^{-1}x)^{-2}

with respect to the uniform measure on SnS^{n}.

Proposition 4.6.

Let Φ:S3→ℝ​ℙ3≅S​O​(3)\Phi:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{3}\cong SO(3) denote the map which identifies antipodal points of S3S^{3}. For any M∈S​O​(3)M\in SO(3) and κ∈[0,1)\kappa\in[0,1), there exists a symmetric positive definite matrix ΛM,κ∈ℝ4×4\Lambda_{M,\kappa}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4} such that if X∼A​C​G3​(ΛM,κ)X\sim ACG_{3}(\Lambda_{M,\kappa}), then Φ⁡(X)∼𝒞3​(M,κ)\Phi(X)\sim\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa).

For a proof see Appendix B.

When n=2n=2 or n=3n=3, Eq. (14) for the Jacobian of the Cayley transform simplifies to 23​n​(n−1)/4​(1+‖ϕ‖2)1−n2^{3n(n-1)/4}(1+\|\phi\|^{2})^{1-n}. One consequence of this fact is that 𝒞n​(In,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(I_{n},\kappa) is the pushforward of a Cauchy distribution (multivariate in the case n=3n=3) under the Cayley transform. This fact makes it possible to compute the KL divergence of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) from the uniform distribution on S​O​(n)SO(n) in these cases.

Proposition 4.7.

For n=2,3n=2,3 the KL divergence of 𝒞n​(M,κ)\mathcal{C}_{n}(M,\kappa) from the uniform distribution is given by

KL(𝒞2(M,κ)∥US​O​(2))\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}(\mathcal{C}_{2}(M,\kappa)\;\|\;U_{SO(2)}) =−log⁡(1−κ2)\displaystyle=-\log(1-\kappa^{2})
KL(𝒞3(M,κ)∥US​O​(3))\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}(\mathcal{C}_{3}(M,\kappa)\;\|\;U_{SO(3)}) =−log⁡(1−κ2)−2​log⁡(1−κ)−2​κ.\displaystyle=-\log(1-\kappa^{2})-2\log(1-\kappa)-2\kappa.

For a proof see Appendix C.

Thus when learning a distribution of cellular sheaves with special orthogonal restriction maps in our BSNN, for the cases where the stalk dimension dd is 22 or 33, we are able to use Eq. (9) to estimate the ELBO by plugging in the expressions for the KL divergence from Proposition 4.7. When d≥4d\geq 4, we estimate the ELBO by simply using Eq. (10).

5 Node Classification Experiments

We compare our Bayesian sheaf neural networks (BSNN) against the sheaf neural networks (NSD) from [6] on the WebKB datasets, a set of real-world web-page datasets. These datasets have low edge-homophily coefficients, that is, there are relatively few edges which connect nodes belonging to the same class [58]. This is a type of graph data where sheaf neural networks are expected to outperform traditional graph neural networks. See Appendix D for further details on the datasets. To study the performance of our Bayesian sheaf models when training data is limited, we use 10 fixed splits of the datasets, each of which contains 32%/20%/48%32\%/20\%/48\% of the nodes for training, validation, and testing respectively. For a given hyperparameter configuration, each model is trained and evaluated on 10 fixed splits of the data and we compute the average validation accuracy. Identical hyperparameter sweeps are performed for each model. For the hyperparameter configuration that yields the best validation accuracy for a model, we train and evaluate the model on the 10 splits for 30 different random seeds. We report the mean test accuracies along with the standard deviation of the test accuracies across the 30 random seeds in Table 1. For each type of restriction map (diagonal, special orthogonal, and general linear), we compare the results of the BSNN model against the NSD model. The higher test accuracy is bolded, and further, a blue entry denotes that a Wilcoxon signed rank test indicates a statistically significant difference for a pp-value threshold of p=0.05p=0.05. We also include results for a graph convolutional network (GCN) as a baseline comparison.

Additionally, to examine the sensitivity of the Bayesian and deterministic sheaf models to the hyperparameter selections, we report the mean test accuracy across all hyperparameter configurations in Table 2.

5.1 Results

Though the results are mixed in the case of diagonal restriction maps, the S​O​(d)SO(d)-BSNN outperforms the corresponding O⁡(d)O(d)-NSD model on all three datasets, and the Gen-BSNN significantly outperforms the corresponding Gen-NSD on all three dataset. This suggests that the comparative advantage of our Bayesian approach to learning cellular sheaves is more pronounced for sheaves with a greater number of parameters. We also note that on each of the three WebKB datasets, the best test accuracy out of all the models is attained by one of our BSNNs. Moreover, the standard deviation of the reported test accuracies for each BSNN is lower than the corresponding NSD model with the same type of restriction map in all but one case, showing that our BSNN models are less sensitive to the effects of random weight initializations.

From Table 2, the advantage of each BSNN model over the corresponding NSD model when considering the entire range of hyperparameters is definitive. For every type of restriction map and dataset, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test for a pp-value threshold of p=0.05p=0.05 indicates a statistically significant difference between the results of the BSNN model and the corresponding NSD model. Thus we observe that the BSNN models maintain good performance over a much wider range of hyperparameters when compared with the NSD model with the same type of restriction maps.

6 Conclusion and Future Directions

In this work, we have introduced Bayesian sheaf neural networks: novel sheaf neural networks in which the sheaf Laplacian is a random latent variable, and where the loss function used in training contains a Kullback-Leibler divergence regularization term. Not only does this allow one to quantify uncertainty of the model arising from the learned sheaf, but we show that for node classifications tasks with limited training data, our BSNN models outperform deterministic sheaf models. Additionally, our experiments suggest that the BSNN models are more robust to different choices of hyperparameters and weight initializations than the corresponding deterministic sheaf models.

We hope that this paper encourages further work on stochastic sheaf neural networks. We briefly mention some possible future directions. Different priors for the distribution of sheaf Laplacians could be suitable for the BSNN depending on the graph dataset, in particular, depending on the level of edge homophily. Although we view the underlying graph as fixed in this paper, one could view it probabilistically and combine our work with the approach taken in [56]. Lastly, similar to the continuous-time version of the sheaf diffusion network that was studied in [6], a continuous-time version of the BSNN could be considered, where the sheaf Laplacian is a stochastic process.

Proposition B.1 (Area formula).

Let f:ℝn→ℝmf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be 11-to-11 and continuously differentiable. For any Borel subset A⊆ℝnA\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n},

∫AJ​f​(x)​λn​(𝑑x)=∫f⁡(A)ℋn​(𝑑y).\int_{A}Jf(x)\lambda^{n}(dx)=\int_{f(A)}\mathcal{H}^{n}(dy).

for all Borel measurable g:ℝm→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} for which one side of (16) exists.

Equip S​O​(n)SO(n) with the metric induced by the Frobenius norm ‖A‖=tr⁡(A𝖳​A)\|A\|=\tr(A^{\mathsf{T}}A). Since left (or right) multiplication on S​O​(n)SO(n) is an isometry, it follows that the Hausdorff measure is a left (and right) translation invariant measure on S​O​(n)SO(n). Moreover, if d=n⁡(n−1)/2d=n(n-1)/2 denotes the dimension of S​O​(n)SO(n), then ℋd\mathcal{H}^{d} is a locally finite measure on S​O​(n)SO(n), and thus is a Haar measure by Haar’s theorem.

Hence, Proposition B.1 yields a change of variables formula for they Cayley transform. For example, if XX is a uniformly distributed random variable on S​O​(n)SO(n), then C−1​(X)C^{-1}(X) has density p⁡(x)=J​C~​(x)p(x)=J\widetilde{C}(x) with respect to the Lebesgue measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Appendix C KL Divergence Calculations

Recall that we assume that the variational distribution qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y) factors as qϕ​(ℱ|X,y)=∏u​⊴​eqϕ​(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y) over all incident node-edge pairs u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e, and that we use a prior pθ​(ℱ)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}) which also factors in the same manner pθ​(ℱ)=∏u​⊴​epθ​(ℱu​⊴​e)p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F})=\prod_{u\trianglelefteq e}p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}). As a consequence of the chain rule for KL divergence, see for example [17, Theorem 2.5.3], we have

KL(qϕ(ℱ|X,y)∥pθ(ℱ))=∑u​⊴​eKL(qϕ(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)∥pθ(ℱu​⊴​e)).\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}))=\sum_{u\trianglelefteq e}\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})).

Hence it suffices to be able to compute KL(qϕ(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)∥pθ(ℱu​⊴​e))\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})) for all u​⊴​eu\trianglelefteq e.

In the cases where we learn diagonal or general linear sheaf restriction maps, KL(qϕ(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)∥pθ(ℱu​⊴​e))\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})) is a KL divergence of a normal distribution with diagonal covariance from a standard normal distribution. The KL divergence of a normal distribution 𝒩⁡(μ,diag⁡(σ2))\mathcal{N}(\mu,\diag(\sigma^{2})) with mean μ∈ℝd\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and σ2∈ℝd\sigma^{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from the standard normal distribution is

KL(𝒩(μ,σ2)∥𝒩(0,1))=−12∑i=1d(1+log(σi2)−μi2−σi2).\textnormal{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})\;\|\;\mathcal{N}(0,1))=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\big(1+\log(\sigma^{2}_{i})-\mu_{i}^{2}-\sigma_{i}^{2}\big). (18)

In the case where the restriction maps are special orthogonal, and the stalk dimension dd is 22 or 33, we compute KL(qϕ(ℱu​⊴​e|X,y)∥pθ(ℱu​⊴​e))\textnormal{KL}(q_{\phi}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e}|X,y)\;\|\;p_{\theta}(\mathcal{F}_{u\trianglelefteq e})) using Proposition 4.7, which we now prove.

Appendix D Experimental Details

All experiments were run on a NVIDIA Tesla K80 GPU with two Intel Xeon E5-2637 CPUs with 64GB of memory. Hyperparameter tuning was done using Weights & Biases [4] to perform a grid search over the hyperparameter configurations described in Table 3. The neural sheaf diffusion (NSD) models from [6] were implemented using the code available at https://github.com/twitter-research/neural-sheaf-diffusion. Our code is available at https://github.com/patrick-gillespie/bsnn.

D.1 WebKB Dataset Descriptions

The Texas, Cornell, and Wisconsin datasets are web page datasets for the computer science departments of the respective universities. Each dataset is a graph in which nodes represent web pages and edges represent hyperlinks between them. In all datasets the node features are 17031703−-dimensional bag-of-word representations of the web pages, and each node belongs to one of the five classes: student, project, course, staff, and faculty. The Texas dataset contains 183 nodes and 325 edges. The Cornell dataset contains 183 nodes and 298 edges. The Wisconsin dataset contains 251 nodes and 515 edges.
